content:
Hello all.

I'm a retired software developer and one-time mathematics undergraduate. For several years I contributed a lot to the free, open-source sound recording and editing program, Audacity. My work there began with (1) an improved algorithm for noise reduction, and (2) a simple spectral editing feature, which required me to think in terms of both time and frequency domain. (And I did much else to improve program quality, but most of the work was not especially mathematical.)

Now keeping my mind occupied with topics in logic and founcations of mathematics. And I'm learning the applications of dependent type theory to automated proofs -- first with experiments in David Christiansen and Daniel Friedman's small Pie language as described in The Little Prover. (Proving "no Nat is both even and odd" and the exhaustive trichotomy of m < n, m = n, m > n with only Peano arithmetic is a bit of work!)

Now I am working through Theorem Proving in Lean and attempting exercises.

I think I have found a bug in tactics! See below. I have not found a way to prove contradiction, but I did get an incorrect proof state in which progress can't be made.

  -- bug in apply And.intro ?
variable (p : Prop)
example : p ∧ False ↔ False := by
  apply Iff.intro
  · simp [*]
  · -- goal is ⊢ False → p ∧ False
    apply And.intro
    -- Tactic incorrectly succeeds, goal is ⊢ p,
    -- and the only hypothesis is p : Prop
    sorry

-- Correct and successful proof
example : p ∧ False ↔ False := by
  apply Iff.intro
  · simp [*]
  · intro; apply And.intro <;> contradiction

From the apply tactic's documentation:

apply e tries to match the current goal against the conclusion of e's type. If it succeeds, then the tactic returns as many subgoals as the number of premises that have not been fixed by type inference or type class resolution.

The type of And.intro is {a b : Prop} → a → b → a ∧ b. So apply And.intro is matching b → a ∧ b against False → p ∧ False. Accordingly, you get one remaining subgoal, which is that for a (which was matched against p).
Getting to a proof state where progress cannot be made does not mean that there is a bug in a tactic. It means that your proof strategy did not work.
What is confusing here is that we think that the conclusion of And.intro is a ∧ b, but for Lean it can also be b → a ∧ b.

Riccardo Brasca said:

What is confusing here is that we think that the conclusion of And.intro is a ∧ b, but for Lean it can also be b → a ∧ b.

Of course. It's clear now that the "conclusion" of the before goal is not unique when it's a curried function type. Sorry to bother!

I discovered this while devising a tactic macro (with recursion) that can solve many of the propositional calculus exercises in chapters 3 and 4 in a single line. That, after I had worked through those exercises once before, using longer term proofs instead.
